name: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1816 (Treaty of the Chickasaw Council House)
promises: Article 2: the Chickasaw ceded all land north of the Tennessee River and relinquished territory south of it east of a line from Caney Creek to Gaines's road and Cotton Gin Port on the Tombigbee.
Article 3: $12,000 a year for ten years, and $4,500 within sixty days of ratification for improvements on the ceded lands.
Article 4: four tracts reserved to the Chickasaw Nation for George Colbert, Appassan Tubby, John McCleish and Levi Colbert, to revert to the United States if abandoned.
Article 5: the line south of the Tennessee to be marked by commissioners attended by two Chickasaw, with due notice to the Nation.
Article 7: at the Chickasaw request, no more licences for pedlars in the nation, and goods brought in contrary to it forfeited.

breaches.what: In a suit under the jurisdictional act of June 7, 1924, the Court of Claims found that $2,000 Congress had appropriated for a treaty obligation of September 20, 1816 was left unexpended, and held the Chickasaw Nation entitled to recover it. It then set the Nation's whole recovery of $22,858.78 off against gratuities and dismissed the petition, so nothing was paid.

today: The Court of Claims found money due under this treaty left unexpended but offset it, with the rest of the Nation's recovery, against gratuities (103 Ct. Cl. 1, 1945; 105 Ct. Cl. 225, 1946). The Chickasaw Nation's Commission dockets (267 to 270) concern later matters such as the Leased District, Choctaw freedmen allotments and Civil War annuities. The 1818 treaty paid Appassan Tubby $500 for his Article 4 reserve and confirmed the Colbert and McCleish reserves to the individuals in fee (kappler-182).

plain.promised: The Chickasaw gave up land north of the Tennessee River for $12,000 a year for ten years and $4,500 for improvements, kept four small reserves, and won a ban on licensed pedlars.
plain.happened: The Court of Claims found in 1945 that $2,000 Congress set aside for a treaty obligation of this date was left unexpended, and held the Chickasaw Nation entitled to it. The Nation also says Jackson pressed the cession.
plain.today: Nothing was paid: the court set the Nation's whole award against gratuities the government had spent for it. The Chickasaw Nation tells this history on its own site.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation says that on September 20, 1816 the Chickasaw ceded close to six million acres in what is now southwestern Tennessee and northern and western Alabama for a $12,000 annuity over ten years, after Andrew Jackson told them the hunt was over, even though they had fought beside him against the Creeks and held a 1794 charter from President Washington guaranteeing their land.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for Chickasaw (Court of Claims index, every case 1884 to 1946 grepped for 1816 and 1818) and 'Chickasaw Council House', 'Chickasaw September 20, 1816' (ICC). Found the Court of Claims ruling of January 8, 1945 (103 Ct. Cl. 1, No. K-544) on an unexpended $2,000 under this treaty, now recorded as a breach. The 1945 opinion does not say which article the $2,000 came from, and case.law does not print the special findings (Finding No. 5) that would say; this treaty's Article 3 sums are $12,000 a year and $4,500. The Supreme Court decision of November 5, 1945 that sent the case back on which gratuities were used was not opened; it is described here only from the Court of Claims order of January 7, 1946.
compensation: Nothing was paid. The Court of Claims held, in 1945 and again in its order of January 7, 1946 after the Supreme Court sent the case back on which gratuities were used, that the Chickasaw Nation was entitled to recover $22,858.78 on its claims, including $2,000 under this treaty, and that the United States could set off a like sum of gratuities spent for the Nation, so the petition was dismissed.
